2

4	
5	## 0. Overlap verdict (headline)
6	
7	**They overlap heavily.** The YAML story-card system was born at commit `8718e5e` on **2025-06-27 15:49** ("docs: Migrate TODO.md to YAML story cards and refine backlog"), and full console transcripts continue for another 16 days, ending **2025-07-12 ~22:47** (`day-021.md`, last commit `f5f6e9e`). Story-card-era development is therefore covered by **12 transcript files** (`day-010` … `day-021`) totalling **~7.3 MB / ~820k tokens** — roughly **70% of the entire diary by volume sits inside the card era.**
8	
9	The migration decision itself is captured verbatim, not merely implied: `day-011.md` lines ~8985–9600 contain the user's provoking message, Gemini's proposal, the acceptance criteria rewrite, and the commit that created `stories/`. There is no gap to bridge on the near side; the gap is on the *far* side — transcripts stop on 2025-07-12 while card-driven work ran on through 2025-07-13/14 (the `validate-filter-values` and `filter-by-sample-flag` stories were marked `done` on 07-13, and the "YOLO mode retrospective" landed 07-14) with **no transcript coverage**. 106	## 4. Intent recoverability
107	
108	Sampled `day-002.md` (2025-04-13, first real transcript, 195 KB / 3687 lines / 39 user turns): opening 150 lines read in full, plus an index of all user turns.
109	
110	**Verdict: the dialogue carries a class of information git does not preserve at all.** Git shows *what the tree became*; the transcript shows *what was proposed, rejected, and why* — including proposals that never reached a commit and therefore left no trace anywhere else.
111	
112	The opening 60 lines alone contain: a rejected `requirements.txt` (never committed, so invisible to git), a rejected `bookminder/core` + `tests/` layout, and the requirements dialogue that produced the project's actual scope. Three short illustrative utterances:
113	
114	> `> I don't know yet... did you gather requirements in a dialog with me?`
115	
116	— the user refusing to let the agent guess at structure; this single line is the origin of the `<requirements_gathering>` section now in `CLAUDE.md`.
117	
118	> `> 1. List books, if possible by last read. I'd like to talk to LLMs like Claude about the books that I am reading on my iPhone. Then we should be able to talk about last chapter that I read. Or about new nighlight I made since we last spoke.`
119	
120	— the actual product motivation, stated once, in prose, never restated in a commit message.
121	
122	> `> W8!!! what are you doing in `claude-dev-log-diary`?! I store there transcripts of our session history that I manually copy from command line. You shouldn't concern` … (line 889)
123	
124	— the origin of the `<file_operations>` rule "Never access `claude-dev-log-diary/` without explicit permission". A one-line guardrail in `CLAUDE.md`; here is the incident that caused it.
125	
126	And from `day-011.md` line ~9018, the message that created the story-card system:
127	
128	> `> w8, waht are you doing? The first scenario should be CR (was previously completed, but we are extending it. But you've marked the Better Errror Handling as [CR], but that's already completed. Our TODO list is getting unweildy... check @vision.md for a proposal how to handle stories with YAML. Let me know it that makes sense and if co, you can star using it with what we have`
129	
130	The commit `8718e5e` records "Migrate TODO.md to YAML story cards and refine backlog". It does not record that the migration was triggered by status-tag confusion in a TODO list that had become unwieldy, that `vision.md` already held the proposal, or that the user asked the agent to sanity-check the idea before adopting it. All three live only here.
131	
132	**Signal density estimate: high, and it rises over time.** 1,772 user turns across the corpus (`^> ` marker; Gemini files under-count — their prompts use a box-drawn `│ >` form, so `day-015`/`day-016` show 0 spuriously). `day-020` alone has 717 user turns in 291k words — roughly one user intervention per 400 words, i.e. a genuinely conversational session rather than a monologue. The user's turns are predominantly *corrective and interrogative* ("what's core? and conf?", "explain how you'd came up with these specific version numbers?", "Did you run test in RED phase?!?", "I don't want to commit the empty `__init__.py` files! Why do we have them again?") — exactly the utterances that encode design rationale.
133	
134	**Swarm-processing this is very likely to recover rationale that exists nowhere else.** Specifically recoverable: the provenance of nearly every rule in `CLAUDE.md` (most were written *in response to an observed failure*, and the failure is on tape); rejected designs; the `--flag`→`--filter` rename debate; why `list-recent-books.yaml` is currently `reopened`. The `gemini-summary-*` files are a poor substitute — they are third-hand prose written for a different purpose (calibrating Gemini's communication style to the user) and they compress 195 KB into ~12 KB, discarding precisely the corrective turns that matter.
135

1	# The BookMinder BDD Style Guide
2	
3	A prescriptive guide to working in this project's style. Each rule carries its motivation. Follow the guide top-down: §1 is why the style exists, §2 the rules, §3 the moves in practice, §4 what violation looks like, §5 the known deviations awaiting repair.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Why this style exists
8	
9	Two motivations — a way of working, and a root principle the whole method grows from.
10	
11	**The partnership.** The point of pairing is having a partner to bounce ideas off: what's the next step? how do we define the test? how do we minimize the surface area of the implementation? what are the minimal constraints to express in a spec to get the desired behavior in the next step? That conversation *is* the discipline of pairing in BDD style. Every rule about small increments, RED-first, and one-behavior-per-commit exists to keep that conversation concrete: each "what next" must resolve into a small failing spec before anyone writes implementation.
12	
13	**The root principle: requirements nailed in a falsifiable way.** A requirement written as prose can be agreed with; encoded as a spec, it can fail. That is the entire basis of doing BDD here, and the method's structure follows from it:
14	
15	- *Executable specification* — because only an executable statement of a requirement is falsifiable. When cloud detection was wrong, the corrected understanding landed as the ZSTATE×ZISSAMPLE truth table in unit specs: documentation that fails when it stops being true.
16	- *GOOS-style layers, with separation enforced* — because each requirement must live at the layer that can falsify it: pure logic where equality can be exact, library behavior against real Apple data, CLI behavior as coordination.
17	- *Delegation as a specified contract* — where one layer delegates to another, the delegation is itself a requirement, so it too gets a falsifiable encoding: the CLI imports the library's filter vocabulary rather than owning a copy, and the acceptance specs mock the library precisely to demonstrate that the CLI delegates to it. The mock is not test convenience; it is the requirement "CLI hands this to the library" written so it can fail.
18	- *Minimal coupling of spec to implementation* — because a spec coupled to internals can fail for reasons that aren't requirement violations, which corrupts the signal. The art is slicing the problem so each spec constrains exactly the contract it is about, and nothing else.
19	
20	**The setting that makes it matter: long-term evolution, not one-shotting.** Apple Books' schema shifts under the tool with every release, so the problem cannot be one-shotted from pretraining or memory — it must be *maintained*. The specs are the durable record of what was learned about a moving target, and the suite is what makes next month's change safe.
21	
22	**Code is a liability; specs are the requirement.** A spec earns its place by constraining the implementation; an implementation earns its place by being demanded by a spec. When they conflict, code loses — deleted, never grandfathered in behind a retroactive test. **A test written to cover existing code is not a spec; it is an alibi.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 2. The principles
27	
28	### 2.1 The spec tree is the requirements document
29	
30	Prose documentation rots silently (this repo's own README still advertises unbuilt features); a spec that stops describing reality *fails*. So the suite is built to be read: `pytest --spec` renders it as living documentation, and every naming rule serves that rendering.
31	
32	- Story yaml → `describe_` → `it_`, in lockstep: `filter-by-cloud-status.yaml` → `describe_bookminder_list_with_filter` → `it_filters_by_cloud_status`. Traceability is checked by reading, not tooling — so the sentence must actually read.
33	- Flat two levels, because the function or command name already *is* the context. The initial RSpec-cargo-cult nesting (`describe_book_library / describe_when_listing_books`) was deleted: a "when" layer that adds no information makes the `--spec` output restate itself.
34	- `describe_` names the feature or command, never a test category, mechanism, or directory — because the describe block is the story's name in the documentation, not a free identifier. (Both the lapse and the reorg broke exactly this: §4g, §5.)
35	- New behavior means a new `describe_`/`it_`, never a repurposed one. A block, once it names a completed story, is owned by that story.

37	Docstrings: **pending skipped specs only.** A not-yet-implemented scenario carries the story's `when:/then:` as docstring with `@pytest.mark.skip` and a concrete-blocker reason; the docstring is deleted in the same commit that implements the body. The skip is how unfinished scenarios stay visible in `--spec` as backlog while the suite stays green. Once implemented, the code IS the specification — a second copy of the scenario means one can silently rot, and the one that rots is always the prose. The Gherkin arc proves the rule was fought for, not assumed: Gemini expanded acceptance docstrings into full Gherkin, the author restored terse form, then deleted the docstring entirely — "its purpose is now served by the YAML story card". 39	### 2.2 Mock rules follow from what the test is — definitional, not preferential
40	
41	"May I mock here?" is answered by the *kind* of test, and the answer follows from what each kind's subject is, not from taste:
42	
43	- **Pure-logic specs** — zero I/O. Data stubs, not mocks of collaborators, because pure functions have none: `row_stub(**overrides)` defaults every field so each spec names only what it is about — `_row_to_book(row_stub(ZSTATE=6, ZISSAMPLE=0))` reads as a truth-table row, and irrelevant fields would be noise hiding the variable under test.
44	- **Collaborator specs** — real fixtures, no mocks, *ever*. Definitional: the collaborator (the SQLite file, the plist, the container layout) is the subject. Mocking it would verify your own stub — a tautology; the whole point is that your beliefs about the collaborator may be wrong. Edge cases use genuinely broken resources: `corrupted_db_user` contains an actual zero-byte SQLite file.
45	- **Coordination specs** — `CliRunner` plus mocks of the library functions the CLI owns the interface to. This is the London-school seam: assert the conversation — `mock_list_recent.assert_called_once_with(user=None, filter=None)`, `format` called once per book in order, citing GOOS explicitly — never output strings, because the CLI's responsibility is coordination, and string assertions test the formatter *through* the CLI, coupling two layers so one behavior change breaks two suites.
46	- **Exactly ONE subprocess wiring test.** Learned the hard way: converting all CLI tests to `CliRunner` silently removed the only coverage of `bookminder/__main__.py`, since in-process invocation never touches the entry point; the revert fixed the count at one — wiring can only be verified by running the wiring, and a second subprocess test re-tests behavior, slowly.
47	
48	Fixtures enter through the front door. The `--user` parameter doubles as the test seam: specs pass a synthetic `$HOME` whose directory tree replicates Apple's container layout path-for-path. The `monkeypatch` of `_books_plist` was deleted in its favor — "No more monkeypatching needed" — because patching a private name couples the spec to an implementation identifier *and bypasses the path-construction code you claim to test*. Each persona home (`never_opened_user`, `fresh_books_user`, `legacy_books_user`, `corrupted_db_user`, `test_reader`) encodes one environmental hypothesis, observed on a real machine rather than imagined — the fixture directory is itself a readable catalogue of the edge cases the product handles.
49	
50	**Known deviation — the four-layer directory taxonomy is not the style.** The `specs/{unit,integration,acceptance,e2e}` split at HEAD, with its `__init__.py` layer contracts, was a one-day reorganization whose own post-mortem judges it misconceived: *taxonomy is discovered, not imposed*; mockist tests ARE unit tests even when they exercise higher-level components, so the mock rules above do not map onto directories. The constitution never adopted the split, and the reorg forced mechanism-named describe blocks (`describe_list_recent_books_integration`) that violate §2.1. The intended shape is **concern-based**: one spec file per module or command (`cli_spec.py`, `apple_books/library_spec.py`), tests within it ranging naturally from helper to feature — which is exactly what the describe/it structure expresses. Until the repair (§5): follow the mock rules by test kind, do not extend the taxonomy, and never let a directory name leak into a `describe_`.
51	
52	### 2.3 Assertion strength is calibrated to the test kind, and maximal for each
53	
54	- **Pure functions: exact equality of the whole output.** `assert format(book) == "Test Book - Test Author (42%) • Sample ☁️"` — the whole output is the contract; substring checks let format regressions ship. One equality assertion subsumes several partials: the dedicated indicator-ordering test was deleted as redundant once whole-string equality pinned order, content, and absence in a single expression. Where the property is genuinely relational, assert the relation: `query.index("WHERE") < query.index("ORDER BY")`.
55	- **Fixture-backed specs: exact sets of the known fixture census** — `assert sample_titles == expected_samples` — because the census is known, so anything weaker throws information away. Every loop assertion is preceded by a non-emptiness guard (`assert len(cloud_books) > 0`), because a `for` over an empty result asserts nothing, and returning nothing is the exact failure the test exists to catch.
56	- **Coordination specs: assert the call; configure nothing you don't assert.** An unused `return_value = []` was deleted because "the default MagicMock is sufficient" — unused stubbing implies the test cares about something it never checks; every line of setup must be load-bearing.
57	- **Error paths: assert which specific path fired.** The error-path spec distinguishes "No BKLibrary database found in:" from the generic message; the scar behind that rule: an untracked fixture directory kept a generic raises-check green for the wrong reason for ~10 days. A test that can pass for the wrong reason is not a specification.
58	- **Diagnostics hand you the counterexample**: `f"Expected cloud book: {book['title']}"` — a failing spec should deliver the falsifying datum, not a boolean.
59	- **Never assert the absence of a problem.** A test asserting output ≠ three hardcoded titles was deleted: it "tested the absence of a problem rather than presence of correct behavior." Negative space is unbounded; a negative assertion constrains nothing. Corollary: never assert about data you never injected — a `not in` check against your own stub is unfalsifiable by construction (§4e).
60	- **Test-data realism is an intent signal.** Boundary specs use `B1`/`A1` — the data is a token, and realistic titles would falsely suggest content matters; fixture-backed specs use real titles because there the data *is* the point. 0-1-many sizing throughout.
61	- **Never depend on the developer's machine.** The first spec file read the author's actual library and cost three commits to make CI pass: a spec that only passes on one machine specifies that machine.
62	
63	### 2.4 Minimalism by deletion; defensiveness requires evidence
64	
65	The constitutive example: a real bug (valid un-downloaded books silently excluded) was fixed by *deleting* the untested `os.path.exists` guard and the blanket `except Exception` — "removing implementation that lacked tests rather than adding tests retroactively" — reaching 100% coverage by subtraction. Untested code is unspecified behavior that can be wrong invisibly; retrofitting tests would only ratify it.
66	
67	Coverage is a residue of good specs, never a target. The author named "Coverage-Driven Development" as an anti-pattern after living it: one commit reached 100% by pointing the DB path at `/dev/null` to hit an except branch, and a later one deleted both the handler and its tests because a coverage number, not an acceptance criterion, had driven them. A deliberate drop ships without apology when the coverage moved to the right place.
68	
69	Defensive code needs demonstrated evidence in the actual data — not "could this be NULL?" but "is it NULL in the data I have?", answered by querying the real database. When speculation ships anyway, it is reverted wholesale. What replaces a deleted handler is a loud assumption: `assert BKLIBRARY_DB_FILE is not None` — crash-visible rather than silently handled.
70	
71	Errors, once a story demands them (the user-environments story, with one fixture per scenario): one domain exception, raised by the layer that knows *what* went wrong with the offending path in the message, translated once at the boundary by the layer that knows *how to say it*. The acceptance spec asserts the contract — message shown, no `Traceback` — without coupling to message text.
72	
73	### 2.5 YAGNI operationalized as testability
74	
75	The test for speculation is concrete: a capability the current fixtures cannot falsify is not a feature. `sort_by` was removed as "YAGNI and untestable with single book" — untestable-now *is* the YAGNI detector, and the coverage report doubles as one.
76	
77	Invoking a respected pattern does not exempt a change from needing a demand: One commit consolidated path helpers into a `LibraryPaths` dataclass, explicitly citing GOOS; the next reverted it, because a design improvement no current requirement needs is still speculative structure everyone must maintain. Extraction is welcome the moment a property needs cheap specification: `format_book_list` so output shaping is unit-testable without a subprocess; `_build_books_query` split from I/O so the column census is assertable after a dropped column had broken sample detection (but see §4 for the cost of how it was specified); path resolution moved CLI→library "where it belongs" so the CLI owns no domain knowledge.
78	
79	The same collapse pressure applies to types: `RecentBook` → `BookWithProgress` → a single `Book` TypedDict with `NotRequired` optionals, because each extra type is another conversion and another place to forget a field — and `NotRequired` is what lets a test construct `Book(title=..., author=...)` and say nothing else, so the type system serves minimal test data instead of fighting it. `isinstance` over `cast`: a cast tells the checker to stop looking; a check tells the program what to do.

81	### 2.6 Discipline is a property of the sequence, not the snapshot
82	
83	Every YOLO commit *individually* looks TDD-shaped — "test: add failing unit test…", "minimal implementation…" — while the causal order (story → acceptance RED → inward) was gone (§4). The vocabulary of the discipline survived; its causal structure did not. **You cannot verify this style commit-by-commit; it lives in the ordering.**
84	
85	Practices that keep the sequence auditable:
86	
87	- **Commit after RED, after GREEN, after REFACTOR.** The RED commit records that the falsifier existed before the implementation — the one claim a GREEN snapshot cannot prove. The rule is the author's own amendment, and his practice; it is absent from CLAUDE.md today only as revert collateral (§5).
88	- **Commit labels must tell the truth.** GREEN and REFACTOR land separately because "refactor" is a machine-checkable claim — behavior preserved — and mislabeling destroys the log's audit property: you can no longer tell which commits could have changed behavior.
89	- **Coverage is moved before it is removed.** Library-level filter tests are added explicitly so coverage survives the CLI-spec conversion that follows; library-level edge-case tests land before the duplicate CLI ones are removed. The safety net moves before the trapeze, because the reverse order leaves a window in which the behavior is unspecified, and that window is where regressions are born.
90	- **Revert is a first-class move when provenance is wrong.** Speculative, duplicative, architecturally mistaken, undisciplined: a change made for the wrong reason cannot be fixed by adding changes on top, because the defect is in how it came to exist.
91	
92	### 2.7 The spec suite and the constitution are production artifacts
93	
94	Changes to the tests, and to the rules that govern how tests get written, get the same discipline as product code. The project learned each of these at cost (§4, §5):
95	
96	- **A commit touching specs is reviewed by diff, never by outcome.** "All tests pass, coverage unchanged" cannot validate a change to the tests — the measuring instrument is the thing being modified. A "pure move" claim is a claim to check: one such commit reported a move and 100% coverage while deleting the only falsifiable sample-filter tests and substituting tautologies under the same names.
97	- **Same `it_` name, weaker assertion, is the most dangerous edit in the suite.** `pytest --spec` renders identically before and after; the living documentation keeps its sentence while the proof behind it evaporates. Re-implementing an existing `it_` requires the diff to show the assertion got stronger or equal.
98	- **The patch target is part of the specification.** `mock.patch` replaces a binding *where it is looked up*, not where it is defined, so the target decides what a spec can falsify — and getting it wrong makes the spec unrunnable rather than merely weak. The filter-validation RED patched `bookminder.apple_books.library.SUPPORTED_FILTERS` while `cli.py` from-imports the constant; the GREEN commit re-pointed it to `bookminder.cli.SUPPORTED_FILTERS`, which is where the CLI actually reads it. That correction was mechanical. The review question is not whether the target moved but what the moved target still asserts — here, that the CLI validates against a set it can be handed, while the identity of that set with the library's stays unstated (§5.1). When a GREEN commit edits a RED test, that edit is the thing to review.
99	- **Amend rules files by addressed diff, never wholesale rewrite.** The CLAUDE.md compression fused 248 line-granular lines into one hunk; the revert could then only undo everything, silently destroying the author's own later improvement committed inside the rewritten region. The XML section tags exist precisely so a rule can be located, cited, and patched in isolation — keep them, and keep changes at the granularity you would want to revert at.
100	- **Friction in a discipline document is often its function.** The compression cut checklists and "Run & Verify RED" as cognitive load; the load was the mechanism — the deliberate pause before acting, in a project whose signature failure mode is acting before pausing. Optimize a rules file for behavior produced, not reading comfort.
101	- **Structural work needs an explicit falsifier too.** Before restructuring the suite or the rules, state what it would look like if the change made things worse, and check for that afterwards. The reorg had a goal ("clear separation of test types") with no test for whether it was achieved; its contract docstrings ratified a nine-hour-old arrangement that had not yet survived a single feature.

105	## 3. The practice — play-by-play
106	
107	### Walking skeleton, honest fake
108	
109	The skeleton commit ships the acceptance test *and* a CLI of three hardcoded `click.echo` lines, labeled exactly what it is ("Minimal hardcoded implementation to establish walking skeleton") → the next pushes the fake behind `list_recent_books()` → the one after replaces it with a real SQLite query. Fake data is a legitimate intermediate because the red acceptance test holds the target fixed while the implementation walks toward it. The fake is driven out through unit specs — never by a meta-test that detects it: exactly such a test was deleted with the rule stated in its place, "tolerate RED acceptance tests while building real implementation through unit tests." A red acceptance test on main means feature-in-progress by design ("Red acceptance test = impl. in progress").
110	
111	### The cadence
112	
113	GREEN, then a burst of one-idea refactor commits — each feature landing is followed by two or three of them. Refactoring is the bulk of the work (55 `refactor:` subjects against 17 `feat:` across the feature-building period), and each step is its own revertible unit. Refactor commits are named for the reason and carry the measurement that justifies them ("Reduced from 25 to 22 statements"; "Reduced 8 individual filter tests to 1") — because a refactor that does not state what improved cannot be evaluated, and cannot be reverted with confidence later.
114	
115	RED is committed, and the best RED commits explain themselves: the filter-delegation spec below was committed deliberately failing, with a body explaining exactly why it fails and what property the failure nails. Scenarios not ready to run are committed skipped with their story docstring, so `--spec` shows the backlog while the suite stays green: `--filter cloud` ships with the negation scenario as a skipped placeholder, and a later commit un-skips it — one behavior per increment, the remainder visible but inert.
116	
117	### Revert-and-narrate
118	
119	One revert carries the most instructive body in the repo: "We made a mistake - instead of refactoring the existing CLI tests in cli_spec.py to use mocks, we created duplicate tests in a new file. This wasn't the goal." Full revert; then the redo converts one test per commit, each body explaining what improved — the first even labels itself an intermediate step and announces "the next commit will show a better approach." The revert-then-redo pair turns a mistake into a documented counterexample and exemplar; patching in place would have erased the lesson. The rule it bought: refactor specs in place, never a parallel suite, because two suites specifying one behavior will eventually disagree and then neither is authoritative.
120	
121	### Exact-equality calibration, worked
122	
123	The formatter spec is built by progressive complexity — no attributes → progress → sample → cloud → all — each an exact whole-string equality; the ordering property is asserted relationally when it is the open question, then subsumed once whole-string equality pins it (the ordering test is then deleted "as redundant"). Symmetry as a table: eight near-identical filter tests collapse into one doubly-parameterized matrix over (command × filter), because the CLI is a uniform passthrough and a table makes any asymmetry a visible anomaly instead of a buried inconsistency.
124	
125	### The high-water mark: the filter-delegation spec
126	
127	```python
128	def it_validates_filter_values_and_shows_helpful_error(runner):
129	    with patch('bookminder.apple_books.library.SUPPORTED_FILTERS', {'foo', 'bar'}):
130	        result = runner.invoke(main, ['list', 'all', '--filter', 'baz'])
131	        assert result.exit_code == 1
132	        assert "Invalid filter: 'baz'" in result.output
133	        assert "foo" in result.output
134	        assert "bar" in result.output
135	```
136	
137	The fictitious names are the whole point, and the commit body says so: "mock filter names (foo, bar) to prove that the CLI completely delegates filter knowledge to the library." Real filter names could pass even against a hardcoded CLI list; nonsense values make the property — *the CLI knows nothing about filters* — falsifiable. This is a design decision (the CLI owns no domain vocabulary) specified so that no implementation cleverness can fake it. That is what a London-school boundary spec is for. It is also the last clean RED before the boundary, and it needed one mechanical correction: the patch above targets `bookminder.apple_books.library.SUPPORTED_FILTERS`, a binding the from-importing CLI never reads, so the spec as committed could not have gone green against any implementation of the import style this project keeps; the GREEN commit re-pointed it to `bookminder.cli.SUPPORTED_FILTERS`. The technique survives that intact — fictitious names still prove the CLI validates against whatever set it is handed rather than a list of its own. What neither version states is that the set it is handed *is* the library's (§5.1).

141	## 4. The lapse — anatomy, each failure named as the principle it violated
142	
143	Boundary: 2025-07-13. The lapse proper runs Jul 13–14 ("YOLO mode" per the retrospective), plus one silent casualty during the Jul 21 reorg.
144	
145	**(a) The patch target was corrected; the contract behind it was never written** — *not a violation; an unspecified requirement.* `mock.patch` replaces a binding *where it is looked up*, not where it is defined. `cli.py` reaches its filter vocabulary through `from … import SUPPORTED_FILTERS` — canonical Python, and the style this project keeps — so the name the CLI actually consults is `bookminder.cli.SUPPORTED_FILTERS`. The RED patched `bookminder.apple_books.library.SUPPORTED_FILTERS`, which the CLI never reads: the real four filters would still have been in force, the invalid-filter path would have printed those real names, and `assert "foo" in result.output` would have failed. The spec could not have passed as written, and re-pointing it in the GREEN commit was mechanical necessity, not spec-weakening. What the episode does leave behind is a claim neither version encodes: that the CLI's filter vocabulary *is* the library's, rather than a set that happens to match it. One line states it falsifiably — `assert cli.SUPPORTED_FILTERS is library.SUPPORTED_FILTERS` — and it has never been written (§5.1).
146	
147	**(b) A spec too weak to constrain, then triangulation without a pull** — *violates: assertions maximal per kind; labels tell the truth.* The unit spec asserted only `isinstance(SUPPORTED_FILTERS, set)` and non-emptiness; the implementation satisfied it with `{"dummy"}`; the next commit, labeled `refactor:`, then changed the expectation to the real four values *and* the implementation in one commit. Behavior changed under a refactor label, and there was no moment at which a failing test drove the real values into existence. Contrast the walking skeleton: fake data was permitted there because a red acceptance test was pulling against it; here nothing pulled, so the fake became real by editorial fiat.
148	
149	**(c) Acceptance-first abandoned** — *violates: outside-in; "done" is user-visible.* Two commits land library code plus unit tests together, nothing showing the tests ever failed, and no acceptance test for a user-visible filter until a retrofit the next day, admitting they "should have been created before implementation." Without the outside-in RED there is no executable statement of user-visible done, so "done" regressed to "code exists."
150	
151	**(d) Non-emptiness guards dropped** — *violates: §2.3.* `it_filters_by_sample_status` loops with no guard — green if the filter returns nothing, which is the exact failure it exists to detect. Its guarded sibling from three weeks earlier sits in the same file.
152	
153	**(e) Fake-strength assertions** — *violates: never assert what you never injected.* A spec asserts `"Sample Book" not in result.output` while the mock returns only a regular book — unfalsifiable by construction. The retrofit was worse: `if output and "No books" not in output:` wrapped the assertions, letting the test pass while asserting nothing. A test that cannot fail is not a specification; it is a comment with a runtime cost.
154	
155	**(f) Evidence-free defensiveness returned** — *violates: §2.4.* The lapse shipped `(ZISSAMPLE != 1 OR ZISSAMPLE IS NULL)` with no NULL in any fixture or observed data — the §2.4 failure recommitted verbatim in SQL. It was deleted after checking the fixtures, the same cure as the first time.
156	
157	**(g) Living documentation commandeered** — *violates: describe names the story.* The lapse displaced `describe_bookminder_list_recent_command`'s content to `…_with_fixtures` and reused the vacated name for filter validation: the `--spec` output for a completed story now described a different feature, corrupting the requirements document itself.
158	
159	**(h) Symmetric features, divergent styles** — *violates: the table principle (§3).* `!cloud` specified as passthrough call-assertion, `!sample` as mock-return-plus-output — two idioms for one property, so a reader cannot tell whether the difference means something. Repaired by the parameterized matrix ("Consistency Trumps Cleverness", per the retrospective).
160	
161	**The earlier crack.** Two commits before the boundary, `_build_books_query` is specced by asserting on the SQL string (`"ZTITLE" in query`, `WHERE` before `ORDER BY`). The motivation is real — a dropped column had genuinely broken sample detection, and the commit says the spec "prevents accidental removal of columns" — but by the project's own standard this couples the spec to implementation text when a behavioral alternative (a fixture book whose flags depend on the column) was available. The armor is sincere; the coupling is the first slip, and it predates the official boundary.
162	
163	**Why it happened, per the project's own diagnosis:** optimizing for finishing over demonstrating; architectural decisions taken silently inside test edits; "didn't fully appreciate BookMinder as a benchmark for process, not just a utility." And the structural lesson: each YOLO commit individually wears TDD vocabulary, which is precisely why the sequence property (§2.6) is the only level at which the discipline can be verified at all.
164	
165	**The repair, its silent casualty, and its limit.** The patch-forward repair (retrospective + retrofit, consistency matrix, evidence-based deletion) was followed by the four-layer reorg — and inside it, a casualty visible only at diff level: one commit, under the message "extract acceptance tests from cli_spec to acceptance/cli_spec … Moved all mocked CLI tests", *deleted* the two fixture-based subprocess sample-filter tests — including `it_excludes_samples_from_recent_books`, the only guarded, genuinely falsifiable end-to-end `!sample` test — and created newly-written mock-based versions under `describe_bookminder_acceptance` carrying the *same `it_` names*. The `--spec` output reads identically; the falsifiability is gone. A "pure move" whose diff was never diffed. (The retrofit's restoration tests were fixture-based; the move silently replaced them with mock versions.)
166	
167	**The meta-artifact lapses.** Two further episodes, distinct from YOLO, motivate §2.7. The spec-tree reorganization (2025-07-21) imposed the four-layer taxonomy in a day, ratified it with contract docstrings the contents did not meet, and carried the silent casualty above inside it; the project's post-mortem rules the conception wrong, and the attempted correction (PR #18) collapsed trying to hold two baselines apart and was abandoned. The CLAUDE.md compression (2025-07-24 → reverted 2025-07-31) deleted everything procedural — checklists, "Run & Verify RED", "no implementation without tests" — while keeping everything declarative, having optimized the rules file for reader burden instead of behavior produced; the wholesale revert then destroyed the author's own commit-after-RED improvement along with it. Shared shape: a meta-artifact optimized against a proxy (taxonomic tidiness; reading comfort) at the expense of falsifiability, passing every existing check because the thing changed *was* the checking apparatus.
168	
169	The author judged patch-forward insufficient for the YOLO code regardless: the unmerged PR #18 performs a semantic revert of the entire YOLO output back to the pre-lapse boundary — removing `SUPPORTED_FILTERS`, `validate_filter`, and sample filtering — and TODO.md still lists the three affected stories as needing "proper ATDD reimplementation." The honest repair is delete and re-derive from a failing test — which the restoration branch then demonstrates with explicit `RED:`/`GREEN:` commits.
